entries.name: startswith-left-lies-true#0
entries.script: { X.startsWith(Coll(1)) }  // JVM: TRUE — and this is the answer the probe could not read off the source. The comparison reaches Scala's `==` on boxed numerics, where 1L == 1, so a Coll[LONG] does start with a Coll[INT] of equal values. No throw, no false: an implementation that refuses a mismatched item type here OVER-REJECTS

entries.name: endswith-left-lies-true#1
entries.script: { X.endsWith(Coll(2)) }  // JVM: TRUE, the endsWith twin of #0 — same numeric-equality comparison

entries.name: startswith-arg-lies-true#2
entries.script: { Coll(1, 2).startsWith(If(false, Coll(1), Coll(1L))) }  // JVM: TRUE with the lie on the ARGUMENT instead of the receiver — the comparison is symmetric

entries.name: startswith-empty-receiver-false#3
entries.script: { E.startsWith(Coll(1)) }  // JVM: FALSE — an empty receiver cannot start with a one-element prefix. False for the LENGTH, not for the item type: the type mismatch is still invisible here

entries.name: endswith-empty-receiver-false#4
entries.script: { E.endsWith(Coll(1)) }  // JVM: FALSE, the endsWith twin of #3

entries.name: startswith-empty-arg-true#5
entries.script: { X.startsWith(Coll[Int]()) }  // JVM: TRUE — every collection starts with the empty one, mismatched items or not

entries.name: endswith-empty-arg-true#6
entries.script: { X.endsWith(Coll[Int]()) }  // JVM: TRUE, the endsWith twin of #5

entries.name: startswith-both-empty-true#7
entries.script: { E.startsWith(Coll[Int]()) }  // JVM: TRUE — empty starts with empty. The cheapest row of the family, and the one an element-type gate would still reject
